title: Call the Sabbath a delight (Isaiah 58:13)
hookLine: honor Shabbat by setting your own business aside

cards: Friday night, after services, some synagogues set out a table in the back: cake, tea, fruit, people lingering and talking. It may be called an oneg. A long table of sugar named after a verse of Isaiah.
Oneg is the Hebrew word for delight, and it comes from the end of chapter fifty-eight, the same chapter that challenged the fasting people.
Having asked for justice alongside the fast, the prophet turns to the seventh day, and doesn't call it a duty or a burden. He says: call it a delight.

teach.b: The verse, near the chapter's end: "If thou turn away thy foot from the sabbath, from doing thy pleasure on my holy day; and call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the LORD, honourable."
And it goes on: not doing thine own ways, nor finding thine own pleasure, nor speaking thine own words. At first that sounds like a contradiction. Don't do your own pleasure, and call it a delight?
But the Hebrew word the King James gives as pleasure can also mean business, the things you're chasing. The 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation renders it thy business.
So: turn your foot away. Step off the road you walk every weekday. Set down what you're pursuing, and in the space that leaves, find delight.

The rabbis took even the last phrase seriously: speaking thine own words. In the Talmud, it's read as a guide to Shabbat talk: don't spend the day on deals and errands and the to-do list. Let the conversation rest too.
And the verb is call. It's something you name, and naming it changes how it's lived.

The same hours can be named a day where nothing gets done, or a day of delight. And the promise at the end: then shalt thou delight thyself in the Lord. The delight people give the day comes back to them.
For Jews who keep it, that can mean candles, a good meal, a nap, a walk, a long talk at the table.

how: Jews who keep Shabbat set work and weekday business aside from Friday sundown to Saturday night, marking the day with candles, festive meals, prayer, rest and study; oneg Shabbat, the delight of the Sabbath, is a phrase drawn from this verse.

games.why: "call the sabbath a delight." setting your business aside makes room for the delight.

practice: Look ahead at the next few days and find one hour you could give back: no business, no errands, no to-do list. Ask what would make it a delight and not just a gap: a walk, a meal with someone, a book, a nap, music.
If you keep Shabbat, you can think of one new delight to bring to it this week.
